lesson.title: Position, Velocity, Acceleration: Reading the Full Ladder
lesson.summary: Position, velocity, and acceleration form a chain of successive derivatives, s(t) to v(t) to a(t), and reading all three together at a single instant reveals the complete story of how an object is moving.
lesson.body:
Each of position, velocity, and acceleration answers a different question in isolation: where is the object, how fast is it going, is that speed changing. Looking at any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture. Looking at all three at the same instant is what actually lets you diagnose motion fully: whether the object is moving, which way, and whether it's speeding up, slowing down, or turning around.

The forward direction is differentiation, exactly as built up over the last two chapters: v(t) = s'(t), then a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t), and if you keep going, j(t) = a'(t) = s'''(t). It's also possible to run this chain in reverse, starting from acceleration and working back to velocity and position, but that requires antidifferentiation (integration), a tool developed later; for now the focus stays on reading the ladder from position downward.

Using the same s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t from the last two chapters, here is the complete picture at five instants. At t = 0: s = 0, v = 9, a = -12. At t = 1: s = 4, v = 0, a = -6. At t = 2: s = 2, v = -3, a = 0. At t = 3: s = 0, v = 0, a = 6. At t = 4: s = 4, v = 9, a = 12.

Look closely at t = 2. Position s(2) = 2 says the object is 2 meters from its starting point. Velocity v(2) = -3 says it's moving in the negative direction at 3 m/s. Acceleration a(2) = 0 says that, at this exact instant, velocity is momentarily not changing, which is no accident: a(t) = v'(t), so a(t) = 0 exactly where v(t) has a local maximum or minimum. Here it's a minimum: v(2) = -3 is the most negative velocity the object reaches during this motion, meaning t = 2 is the instant of maximum backward speed. That kind of connection, reading acceleration's zero as a signal about velocity's turning point, is exactly what the next few chapters, speed versus velocity, direction of motion, and speeding up versus slowing down, explore in more depth.
